The other two capstones train a model **from scratch**. This one does the thing
you are far more likely to do in practice: take a model somebody else already
spent a fortune pretraining, and **fine-tune it on your data**.

[\[3.3\]](../../03-advanced-llms/3-mid-post-training/) showed you the mechanics of
SFT — chat templates, and the `-100` mask that puts the loss only on the
assistant's tokens. Here we run the whole thing end to end on a real open model
and a real dataset, and then ask the question people usually skip:

> The loss went down. **What actually changed?**

The answer on this dataset is genuinely interesting, and it is not "the model
learned Gen Z slang."

```{python}
try:
    import bootcamp  # noqa: F401
```

```{python}
import time

import ezpz
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import torch
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

from bootcamp.plotly_theme import apply_theme, COLORS

apply_theme()
torch.manual_seed(0)

DEVICE = ezpz.get_torch_device_type()   # 'cuda' | 'xpu' | 'mps' | 'cpu'
GPU = DEVICE in ("cuda", "xpu")

# Scale the run to the hardware. On a laptop this stays a ~2-minute demo; on a
# GPU node it trains a 4x bigger model for more epochs, which is what you want
# when you are actually trying to answer "does more compute fix this?".
MODEL = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct" if GPU else "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct"
EPOCHS = 4 if GPU else 1
BATCH = 16 if GPU else 8
N_EVAL = 240 if GPU else 80

print(f"device: {DEVICE}  model: {MODEL}")
print(f"epochs: {EPOCHS}  batch: {BATCH}  eval rows: {N_EVAL}")
```

::: {.callout-note title="🖥️ This page is GPU-aware"}
Everything below runs unchanged on a laptop, just smaller. The numbers you see
in *this* rendering were produced on the hardware named above — if it says
`cuda`, a real GPU trained a 360M-parameter model; if it says `cpu` or `mps`,
you are looking at the 135M laptop-scale run.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="🐛 A real bug we hit: batched generation on Apple MPS"}
While scaling this up we tried batching the evaluation generations. On CPU and
CUDA that is a pure speedup. On **MPS** it silently returns *empty strings* for
most of the batch, because `pad_token_id == eos_token_id` for this tokenizer
and left-padding makes the model stop immediately.

The first version of our scaling experiment reported `overlap 0.000` and we
nearly concluded that more training made the model worse. It had not — the
measurement was broken, on one accelerator only.

This is the reason to run the same code on more than one device before you
trust a result, and a good thing to mention in your presentation.
:::

## 📖 The data

[`MLBtrio/genz-slang-dataset`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MLBtrio/genz-slang-dataset)
is 1,779 rows and four columns: the **Slang** term, a short **Description**, an
**Example** sentence, and the social **Context**. It is a single CSV, so we can
skip the `datasets` library entirely and just read it with pandas.

```{python}
URL = ("https://huggingface.co/datasets/MLBtrio/genz-slang-dataset/"
       "resolve/main/all_slangs.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(URL)
df["key"] = df["Slang"].astype(str).str.strip().str.lower()

print(f"{len(df)} rows, {df['key'].nunique()} unique terms\n")
for _, r in df.head(3).iterrows():
    print(f"  {r.Slang!r:12s} -> {r.Description}")
    print(f"  {'':12s}    e.g. {r.Example}\n")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Read the dataset card before you trust the labels"}
The card says the `Example` and `Context` columns were added by "scraping
publicly available websites and using generative AI." So part of your ground
truth is **model-generated**, which means some of it is wrong, and a model that
scores well against it may just be agreeing with whatever model wrote it. No
license is listed either.

None of that makes the dataset useless — it makes it *normal*. Almost every
real dataset has provenance problems like this. Knowing them is the job.
:::

## 🚨 The split that quietly lies to you

Here is the first thing to check on any dataset, and the reason to check it is
sitting in plain sight: there are 1,779 rows but only 1,571 unique terms. **170
terms appear more than once** — `lol` appears five times.

If you shuffle rows and take the last 15% as your test set, some of those
duplicate terms land on *both* sides. The model sees `lol` in training and then
gets graded on `lol` at test time. Your number goes up and your model did not
get better.

```{python}
def split(kind, frac=0.85, seed=0):
    """`random` shuffles ROWS (leaky). `grouped` shuffles TERMS (honest)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if kind == "random":
        idx = rng.permutation(len(df))
        cut = int(frac * len(df))
        return df.iloc[idx[:cut]], df.iloc[idx[cut:]]
    keys = df["key"].unique().copy()
    rng.shuffle(keys)
    keep = set(keys[:int(frac * len(keys))])
    return df[df["key"].isin(keep)], df[~df["key"].isin(keep)]


for kind in ("random", "grouped"):
    tr, te = split(kind)
    leak = te["key"].isin(set(tr["key"])).mean()
    print(f"  {kind:8s} train={len(tr):5d} test={len(te):4d} "
          f"| {leak:.1%} of test terms also appear in train")
```

One in five test terms is contaminated under the naive split. We will train on
the **grouped** split, where that number is exactly zero.

```{python}
train_df, test_df = split("grouped")
train_rows, test_rows = list(train_df.itertuples()), list(test_df.itertuples())
EVAL = test_rows[:N_EVAL]  # fixed held-out slice, used for every number below
```

## 🧩 Prompt format and the `-100` mask

`SmolLM2` is an *instruct* model, so it already ships a chat
template — unlike the bare `gpt2` in [\[3.3\]](../../03-advanced-llms/3-mid-post-training/),
we do not have to invent one. Each row becomes a one-turn conversation whose
assistant reply is the gloss.

```{python}
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)


def render(row, with_answer=True):
    msgs = [{"role": "user",
             "content": f'What does the slang term "{row.Slang}" mean?'}]
    prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False,
                                     add_generation_prompt=True)
    if not with_answer:
        return prompt
    return prompt + f"{str(row.Description).strip()}{tok.eos_token}"


print(render(train_rows[0]))
```

Now the part that makes it SFT rather than plain language modelling: label the
prompt tokens `-100` so the loss ignores them. The model is graded only on the
gloss it was supposed to produce.

```{python}
def encode(row, maxlen=128):
    prompt_ids = tok(render(row, False), add_special_tokens=False).input_ids
    full = tok(render(row, True), add_special_tokens=False).input_ids[:maxlen]
    labels = list(full)
    for i in range(min(len(prompt_ids), len(labels))):
        labels[i] = -100          # <- the whole trick
    return full, labels


ids, labels = encode(train_rows[0])
kept = [tok.decode([i]) for i, la in zip(ids, labels) if la != -100]
print(f"{len(ids)} tokens total, loss computed on {len(kept)} of them")
print("  scored text:", repr("".join(kept)))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the batching / evaluation helpers"
def batches(rows, bs):
    """Pad to the longest sequence in each batch; -100 pads the labels."""
    for i in range(0, len(rows), bs):
        chunk = [encode(r) for r in rows[i:i + bs]]
        n = max(len(a) for a, _ in chunk)
        ids = torch.full((len(chunk), n), tok.pad_token_id)
        lab = torch.full((len(chunk), n), -100)
        att = torch.zeros((len(chunk), n), dtype=torch.long)
        for j, (a, b) in enumerate(chunk):
            ids[j, :len(a)] = torch.tensor(a)
            lab[j, :len(b)] = torch.tensor(b)
            att[j, :len(a)] = 1
        yield ids.to(DEVICE), lab.to(DEVICE), att.to(DEVICE)


@torch.no_grad()
def held_out_loss(model, rows, bs=8):
    model.eval()
    total, n = 0.0, 0
    for ids, lab, att in batches(rows, bs):
        total += model(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=att, labels=lab).loss.item() * len(ids)
        n += len(ids)
    return total / n


@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, rows, max_new_tokens=24):
    model.eval()
    outs = []
    for r in rows:
        enc = tok(render(r, False), return_tensors="pt").to(DEVICE)
        g = model.generate(**enc, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, do_sample=False,
                           pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id)
        outs.append(tok.decode(g[0][enc.input_ids.shape[1]:],
                               skip_special_tokens=True).strip())
    return outs
```

## 📏 A second metric, because loss is not the point

The chess capstone's lesson was that **your loss curve is not your metric**. So
before training, let us define something that measures whether the answer is
*right*, not just whether it is likely: what fraction of the gold gloss's
content words show up in the generated answer?

```{python}
STOP = set("a an the of to is are be been being or and for in on with that this "
           "it its as someone something used describe describing refers term "
           "slang when who very you your".split())


def content_words(s):
    return {w for w in "".join(c.lower() if c.isalnum() else " "
                               for c in str(s)).split()
            if w and w not in STOP and len(w) > 2}


def overlap(generations, rows):
    """Mean fraction of the gold gloss's content words present in the output."""
    vals = [len(g & content_words(gen)) / len(g)
            for gen, r in zip(generations, rows)
            if (g := content_words(r.Description))]
    return float(np.mean(vals))
```

It is a crude metric. Check that it discriminates at all before relying on it —
a scorer that gives everything the same number tells you nothing:

```{python}
gold = [str(r.Description) for r in EVAL]
shuffled = gold[1:] + gold[:1]          # every gloss paired with the WRONG term
print(f"  gloss vs itself        : {overlap(gold, EVAL):.3f}")
print(f"  gloss vs a random gloss: {overlap(shuffled, EVAL):.3f}")
```

## 📊 Before: what the base model already does

```{python}
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL).to(DEVICE)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

t0 = time.time()
base_loss = held_out_loss(model, EVAL)
base_gen = generate(model, EVAL)
base_overlap = overlap(base_gen, EVAL)
base_len = float(np.mean([len(g.split()) for g in base_gen]))
print(f"{MODEL}  ({n_params/1e6:.0f}M params)")
print(f"  held-out loss    {base_loss:.3f}")
print(f"  content overlap  {base_overlap:.3f}")
print(f"  avg answer words {base_len:.1f}   ({time.time()-t0:.0f}s)")
```

## 🔧 Fine-tune

Plain AdamW over ~1,500 examples. No LoRA, no TRL — a full fine-tune of a model
this size fits comfortably, and the point here is that you can see every line of
it.

We measure **after every epoch**, not just at the end, because the interesting
question is not "did it improve?" but "do the loss and the task metric even
agree about *when* it improved?"

```{python}
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-5)

history, curve = [], []
t0 = time.time()
for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):
    model.train()
    order = np.random.default_rng(epoch).permutation(len(train_rows))
    for ids, lab, att in batches([train_rows[i] for i in order], BATCH):
        loss = model(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=att, labels=lab).loss
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step()
        opt.zero_grad()
        curve.append(loss.item())
    ep_loss = held_out_loss(model, EVAL)
    ep_gen = generate(model, EVAL)
    history.append(dict(epoch=epoch, loss=ep_loss,
                        overlap=overlap(ep_gen, EVAL),
                        words=float(np.mean([len(g.split()) for g in ep_gen]))))
    h = history[-1]
    print(f"  epoch {epoch}  held-out loss {h['loss']:.3f}  "
          f"overlap {h['overlap']:.3f}  words {h['words']:.1f}  "
          f"({time.time()-t0:.0f}s)")

print(f"\n{len(curve)} steps in {time.time()-t0:.0f}s on {DEVICE}")
```

```{python}
# The final epoch's numbers are already measured; reuse them rather than
# paying for another pass over the eval set.
ft_gen = generate(model, EVAL)
ft_loss, ft_overlap = history[-1]["loss"], history[-1]["overlap"]
ft_len = history[-1]["words"]

print(f"{'':16s} {'base':>8s} {'fine-tuned':>12s}")
print(f"{'held-out loss':16s} {base_loss:8.3f} {ft_loss:12.3f}")
print(f"{'content overlap':16s} {base_overlap:8.3f} {ft_overlap:12.3f}")
print(f"{'avg words':16s} {base_len:8.1f} {ft_len:12.1f}")

best = min(history, key=lambda h: h["loss"])
peak = max(history, key=lambda h: h["overlap"])
if len(history) > 1 and best["epoch"] != peak["epoch"]:
    print(f"\n  ⚠️  lowest loss at epoch {best['epoch']} ({best['loss']:.3f}), "
          f"but best overlap at epoch {peak['epoch']} ({peak['overlap']:.3f})")
    print("      early-stopping on loss would have picked the wrong checkpoint.")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-slang-finetune
#| fig-cap: "Left: the training loss. Right: the three held-out measurements before and after, each scaled against the larger of its two bars (the real values are printed on top). The loss falls by more than half and the answers get much shorter; whether they get *more correct* is the question worth arguing about."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, column_widths=[0.58, 0.42],
                    subplot_titles=("training loss", "held-out, before vs after"))
fig.add_scatter(x=list(range(1, len(curve) + 1)), y=curve, mode="lines",
                line=dict(color=COLORS["blue"], width=1.5),
                name="train loss", row=1, col=1)
k = 15
if len(curve) >= k:
    sm = np.convolve(curve, np.ones(k) / k, mode="valid")
    fig.add_scatter(x=list(range(k, len(curve) + 1)), y=sm, mode="lines",
                    line=dict(color=COLORS["red"], width=2.5),
                    name=f"{k}-step mean", row=1, col=1)
# The three quantities have different units, so plot each as a fraction of the
# larger of the two bars and print the real value on the bar.
cats = ["held-out loss", "content overlap", "answer length"]
pairs = [(base_loss, ft_loss), (base_overlap, ft_overlap), (base_len, ft_len)]
fmt = ["{:.2f}", "{:.3f}", "{:.1f}w"]
for name, pick, color in (("base", 0, COLORS["red"]), ("fine-tuned", 1, COLORS["blue"])):
    fig.add_bar(x=cats,
                y=[p[pick] / max(p) for p in pairs],
                text=[f.format(p[pick]) for f, p in zip(fmt, pairs)],
                textposition="outside", name=name, marker_color=color,
                row=1, col=2)
fig.update_xaxes(title="step", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(title="loss", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(title="relative to the larger bar", range=[0, 1.25], row=1, col=2)
fig.update_layout(height=400, margin=dict(t=60), barmode="group")
fig.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-slang-epochs
#| fig-cap: "Held-out loss (left axis) and content overlap (right axis) after each epoch. When these two disagree about which epoch was best, the loss is not measuring the thing you care about."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
# With a single epoch (laptop run) there is no trend to draw.
eps = [h["epoch"] for h in history]
f2 = go.Figure()
f2.add_scatter(x=eps, y=[h["loss"] for h in history], name="held-out loss",
               mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color=COLORS["red"], width=2.5))
f2.add_scatter(x=eps, y=[h["overlap"] for h in history], name="content overlap",
               mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color=COLORS["blue"], width=2.5),
               yaxis="y2")
f2.update_layout(
    height=380, margin=dict(t=50),
    xaxis=dict(title="epoch", tickmode="array", tickvals=eps),
    yaxis=dict(title=dict(text="held-out loss (lower better)",
                          font=dict(color=COLORS["red"])),
               tickfont=dict(color=COLORS["red"])),
    yaxis2=dict(title=dict(text="content overlap (higher better)",
                           font=dict(color=COLORS["blue"])),
                tickfont=dict(color=COLORS["blue"]),
                overlaying="y", side="right"),
)
if len(history) > 1:
    f2.show()
else:
    print("single-epoch run — see the GPU rendering for the per-epoch trend")
```

## 🤯 What actually changed

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the comparison code"
for r, b, f in list(zip(EVAL, base_gen, ft_gen))[:6]:
    print(f"{r.Slang!r}  (gold: {str(r.Description)[:52]})")
    print(f"   base: {b[:88]}")
    print(f"   ft  : {f[:88]}\n")
```

::: {.callout-important title="🎯 Mostly format, a little knowledge — and the two metrics disagree"}
Look at the two columns. The base model answers every question with the same
hedging boilerplate — *"The slang term X is a colloquialism that refers to..."* —
and rambles. After fine-tuning it answers in a handful of words, in the clipped
register of the dataset. That is a big, obvious change, and it is most of why
the loss dropped.

Now read the answers. On terms it has **never seen**, many are still confidently,
fluently wrong. Content overlap does improve — real, but far short of "the model
learned Gen Z slang." Most of the loss improvement bought you *voice*, not
*knowledge*.

> **SFT on a small dataset mostly teaches style and format. Knowledge comes
> slowly, if at all.**

A few epochs over 1,500 short examples cannot install many facts the pretrained
model never saw. It *can* teach it how to answer, in what voice, at what length.
Those are different things, and **the loss curve cannot tell them apart** — see
@fig-slang-epochs, where the held-out loss and the task metric peak at
*different epochs*. Had you early-stopped on loss, as almost everyone does, you
would have shipped the wrong checkpoint.

If you need the model to know new facts, you need much more data, much longer
training, or you need to stop fine-tuning and start *retrieving* — which is
exactly what [\[2.9\] RAG](../../02-llms/09-rag-tutorial/) is for.
:::

## 🔬 Proving the leaky split inflates the score

Earlier we picked the grouped split on principle. Now let us pay for a second
training run and show it was not just principle — retrain on the **random**
split and score the leaked and clean test terms separately.

```{python}
lk_train, lk_test = split("random")
lk_train_rows = list(lk_train.itertuples())
seen_keys = set(lk_train["key"])
seen = [r for r in lk_test.itertuples() if r.key in seen_keys][:60]
unseen = [r for r in lk_test.itertuples() if r.key not in seen_keys][:60]

leaky = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL).to(DEVICE)
opt2 = torch.optim.AdamW(leaky.parameters(), lr=3e-5)
order2 = np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(len(lk_train_rows))
leaky.train()
for ids, lab, att in batches([lk_train_rows[i] for i in order2], BATCH):
    leaky(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=att, labels=lab).loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(leaky.parameters(), 1.0)
    opt2.step()
    opt2.zero_grad()

print(f"  loss on test terms SEEN in training : {held_out_loss(leaky, seen):.3f}")
print(f"  loss on test terms NOT seen         : {held_out_loss(leaky, unseen):.3f}")
```

The gap between those two numbers is the size of the lie. Every leaked term
drags the headline metric toward the easier number, and nothing in your training
logs will warn you.

## 🎒 Your turn

1. **Change what you predict.** We trained on `Description`. Train on `Example`
   instead so the model *uses* the slang in a sentence rather than defining it.
   Which is a better demo? Which is easier to score?
2. **Does more data fix the facts?** Scaling the *model* (135M → 360M) and the
   *epochs* helped a little — you can see it in the numbers above. Now scale the
   **data**: train on 10%, 25%, 50%, 100% and plot content overlap against
   dataset size. Extrapolate. How much data would you need for the model to
   actually know the words, and is that a realistic amount to collect?
3. **Beat the fine-tune with retrieval.** Put the gold gloss for the test term
   into the prompt and let the *base* model answer. If that crushes your
   fine-tuned model — and it will — you have demonstrated the single most
   practical result in this bootcamp.
4. **Try a bigger base.** `SmolLM2-360M-Instruct`, or `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`
   from [\[3.3\]](../../03-advanced-llms/3-mid-post-training/). Does the larger
   model already know more slang before you touch it?
5. **Catastrophic forgetting.** Ask the fine-tuned model something unrelated
   ("What is the capital of France?"). Fine-tuning on one narrow, terse dataset
   often wrecks general ability. Measure how much.

::: {.callout-tip title="📊 What to put on the slide"}
@fig-slang-epochs, with the two curves peaking at different epochs, plus three
or four real generations. The strongest version of this talk states the
uncomfortable result out loud: *"our loss got better every way we measured it,
and the epoch with the best loss was not the epoch with the best answers."*
Then show the retrieval baseline beating the whole thing.
:::

## 🚀 Scaling up

Nothing here needs a GPU, but everything here is faster with one, and the same
script scales without modification:

```bash
# one node, all its GPUs
ezpz launch python3 slang_finetune.py --epochs 3 --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct
```

`DEVICE` comes from `ezpz.get_torch_device_type()`, so the same code picks up
`cuda` on Polaris/Perlmutter, `xpu` on Aurora, `mps` on a Mac, and CPU
everywhere else. See
[\[3.1\] Pretraining at Scale](../../03-advanced-llms/1-pretraining-at-scale/)
for how to turn this single-process loop into a distributed one.
